name: Blue-light teeth whitening device

card.summary: LED gadgets sold to whiten teeth with blue light; light helps only as an add-on to peroxide in some studies, and light-only data is lacking.
card.note: No studies of light-only whitening were found.

quick.overview:
Blue-light whitening devices are consumer LED gadgets, some sold to whiten with light alone.

Dentistry uses light with peroxide gel, and reviews of that practice are mixed. No evidence for light-only whitening was found.
quick.mechanism: Whitening is attributed to peroxide breaking down stain molecules. Light is proposed to speed this, though its benefit is debated.
quick.risks: Sensitivity and gum irritation are common with peroxide whitening; light may add heat. Results can fade within months.

lead: A blue-light teeth whitening device is a consumer gadget, often a handheld wand or mouthpiece with LEDs, marketed to brighten teeth, sometimes together with a peroxide gel and sometimes on its own. Whiter teeth are among the most common cosmetic goals; Wikipedia reports that over 100 million Americans had whitened their teeth, spending about $15 billion in 2010 [1]. The category is tied to light-accelerated (power) bleaching in dental offices, which uses halogen, LED or plasma arc lights, typically in the blue spectrum, together with high-concentration peroxide gel [1].

Whitening chemistry is attributed to peroxide breaking down pigment molecules [1]. Reviews of adding light to peroxide bleaching have reached mixed conclusions, and no published trial of whitening by blue light alone was found.

chain: LED light shone on teeth, usually with peroxide gel
Light is proposed to speed up the whitening reaction
Teeth look a few shades lighter and the smile looks brighter
angle.text: People buy the devices to get a whiter smile at home. In professional treatment, light is used to accelerate peroxide bleaching, and consumer kits borrow that idea.

infobox: FDA endorses under 6% hydrogen peroxide or up to 16% carbamide peroxide [1]

paras: Devices vary from handheld LED wands to mouth trays with built-in lights. Many are sold alongside a gel, and some are advertised as working with light alone. Claims come from sellers.

In-office light-accelerated bleaching typically applies 25 to 38 percent hydrogen peroxide gel behind a gum barrier, followed by 6 to 15 minutes of light exposure [1]. Wikipedia reports that used properly, light can increase whitening without more sensitivity, while used improperly it can increase sensitivity and may not beat high-concentration bleaching without light [1]. A 2015 study cited there found light activation did not improve results and could raise tissue temperature [1]. Newer devices are described as emitting less heat and UV [1].

In-office treatment can gain 2 to 7 shades over one or more visits, and bleaching works best on yellow teeth and least on grayish ones [1]. Home strips typically lighten teeth by 1 to 2 shades within several days, and toothpastes gain 1 to 2 shades with continued use [1]. Nearly half the change from an intensive in-office session may be lost within a week through rehydration [1].

Sensitivity is reported in 67 to 78 percent of in-office patients, lasting roughly 4 to 39 days, and peroxide can irritate gums, with poorly fitting trays a common cause of chemical burns [1]. Wikipedia also describes enamel roughening from carbamide peroxide, effects on restorations and the term bleachorexia for an unhealthy repeated pursuit of whiter teeth [1].

No studies found of light-only consumer whitening. Studies of light as an adjunct to peroxide in professional bleaching exist and are mixed [1]. A study in young participants cited on Wikipedia found whitening improved oral-health-related quality of life in areas such as smiling, though sensitivity reduced that benefit [1].

lore.intro: Blue-light whitening is mostly discussed in product marketing and social media; no forum material was located for this entry.

claims.claim: Blue light can whiten teeth on its own or much faster
claims.believers: Marketing and some users state that LED light activates whitening and gives visible results quickly.
claims.experts: Reviews examine light as an addition to peroxide gel and report mixed outcomes; a 2015 study found no improvement from light activation [1]. No studies of light-only whitening were located.
